title: Household inflation, earnings, and consumption diverge across US groups
source_unit: New York Fed Economic Heterogeneity Indicator for demographic, economic, and geographic group consumption baskets and outcomes
geography: United States national indicators, with metro, regional, demographic, and urban/rural groupings

denominator.unit: major US metropolitan areas used in the demographic-CPI construction, with smaller cities and towns assigned by census region

observations.method: Demographic expenditure shares from BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey microdata are combined with category and metro CPI inflation; group contributions are aggregated to demographic inflation indexes and compared with overall inflation.
observations.uncertainty: Demographic inflation is an author-constructed estimate, not an official BLS demographic CPI. It assumes people within a metro area face the same category prices and uses expenditure shares from the prior available CEX year; rural estimates use urban regional prices.
observations.subgroup: Race/ethnicity, income, age, education, census region, and urban/rural status.
observations.counterinterpretation: A group inflation gap reflects both expenditure composition and assigned prices; it does not by itself show different realized prices paid by every household or identify a causal policy shock.

denominator.unit: reported comparison benchmark for each earnings-ratio series

noncollege_to_college_earnings.unit: percent of workers with a college degree's earnings

observations.method: National EHI earnings ratios calculated for employed worker groups using BLS-based earnings measures; ratios compare group average earnings to a named benchmark.
observations.uncertainty: Ratios describe earnings among employed workers and do not capture differential employment, hours, occupation, or selection into work. The release is an indicator publication, not a causal decomposition.
observations.subgroup: Race/ethnicity, education, sex, and urban/rural status.
observations.counterinterpretation: A changing earnings ratio may reflect composition, hours, occupations, employment selection, or labor-market composition rather than a change in bargaining power alone.

denominator.unit: balanced Numerator household panel used for receipt-level retail spending indicators

real_high_income_consumption.unit: direction of real retail-consumption change since 2023

real_middle_income_consumption.unit: direction of real retail-consumption change since 2023

real_low_income_consumption.unit: direction of real retail-consumption change since 2023

observations.method: Receipt-level Numerator retail spending is aggregated by demographic group, deflated using demographic-specific inflation indexes, and seasonally adjusted; retail excludes automobiles in the national measure.
observations.uncertainty: Numerator is a market-research receipt and permissioned-email panel rather than a government probability survey. The reported directions are aggregate group trends, not within-household causal changes or evidence that inflation alone caused the divergence.
observations.subgroup: Income, education, race/ethnicity, age, urban status, and census region.
observations.counterinterpretation: Different consumption growth may reflect wealth, income, employment, credit, household composition, product mix, panel composition, or unobserved price and quantity changes.

related_sources.claim: New York Fed EHI landing page, methodology, updates, and downloadable national/regional data.
Related Federal Reserve household price-adaptation and financial-room evidence.

boundary: This record measures constructed demographic inflation, employed-worker earnings ratios, and aggregate receipt-based retail-consumption directions through December/November 2025. It does not establish household-specific prices, policy causality, trust, political action, or a same-household cost-to-behavior chain. The EHI indicators are not official estimates of the Federal Reserve System or FOMC.
